content:
Occupational therapists (OTs) are unsung heroes in arthritis management. They specialise in helping you maintain independence in everyday activities despite joint pain and stiffness. In the UK, OT services are available through the NHS and local councils.

Quick answer: Occupational therapists (OTs) help people with arthritis maintain independence in daily activities. They teach techniques for joint protection, make custom splints, and recommend home adaptations such as grab rails and kitchen aids. OTs also assist with energy management, helping to balance activity and rest. You can access OT services through your GP, rheumatology department, or local council in the UK.

What Does an OT Do for Arthritis?

Joint Protection Techniques

OTs teach you how to use your joints in ways that reduce strain and prevent further damage:

  • Using larger, stronger joints for tasks (carrying bags on forearms rather than fingers)
  • Distributing weight evenly across joints
  • Avoiding sustained gripping and pinching
  • Planning tasks to avoid prolonged activity and fatigue

Splinting

OTs can make custom splints for:

  • Resting splints — worn at night to support joints in a comfortable position
  • Working splints — provide support during daily activities
  • Thumb splints — for base-of-thumb arthritis, very common
  • Wrist splints — stabilise and support inflamed wrist joints

Home Adaptations

OTs assess your home and recommend adaptations:

  • Grab rails in the bathroom and by stairs
  • Raised toilet seats and shower seats
  • Stair lifts or stair rails
  • Kitchen aids — jar openers, tap turners, ergonomic utensils
  • Lever door handles instead of round knobs

Energy Management (Pacing)

OTs help you balance activity and rest to manage fatigue — one of the most debilitating aspects of inflammatory arthritis.

How to Access OT in the UK

Through the NHS

  • Ask your GP for a referral to NHS occupational therapy
  • Many rheumatology departments have OTs as part of their team
  • Hospital-based OTs focus on splints and joint protection

Through Your Local Council

  • Contact your council's adult social care team for a home assessment
  • Community OTs focus on home adaptations and equipment
  • Some equipment and adaptations are provided free through the Disabled Facilities Grant

Useful Equipment from OT

  • Long-handled shoe horn — avoid bending to put on shoes
  • Button hook — fasten buttons with one hand
  • Jar opener — reduces hand and wrist strain
  • Perching stool — sit while doing kitchen tasks
  • Electric can opener, kettle tipper — reduce grip demands

OTs can make a dramatic difference to your daily life with arthritis. Don't hesitate to ask your GP or rheumatology team for a referral.

Practical next steps for Occupational Therapy for Arthritis in the UK

If you came here about Occupational Therapy for Arthritis in the UK, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Quick questions about Occupational Therapy Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
